derivations.claim: Define $S(\theta)=\sum_i\min(\lambda_i,\theta)$ for $0\le\theta\le\max_i\lambda_i$. It is continuous, $S(0)=0$, and $S(\max_i\lambda_i)=\sum_i\lambda_i$. If $0\le\theta_1<\theta_2<\max_i\lambda_i$, some $\lambda_j>\theta_2$, so the $j$-th summand increases strictly and the others do not decrease. Thus for $0<D<\sum_i\lambda_i$, the intermediate-value theorem gives a unique $\theta$ with $S(\theta)=D$.
For $t>0$, $\ln t\le t-1$: if $t\ge1$, integrate $1/u\le1$ on $[1,t]$; if $0<t<1$, use $\ln t=-\int_t^1du/u$ and $1/u\ge1$ on $[t,1]$. Hence $-\ln t+t-1\ge0$.

Fix $0<D<\sum_i\lambda_i$, its $\theta$, and $c=(2\theta\ln2)^{-1}$. If $\lambda_i>\theta$, then for $0<\delta_i\le\lambda_i$, $$\phi_i(\delta_i)-\phi_i(\theta)+c(\delta_i-\theta)=\frac{-\ln(\delta_i/\theta)+\delta_i/\theta-1}{2\ln2}\ge0$$ by step 1.2; the inequality also holds at $\delta_i=0$ because $\phi_i(0)=+\infty$. If $0<\lambda_i\le\theta$, then $\phi_i(\lambda_i)=0$, and for $0<\delta_i\le\lambda_i$, step 1.2 gives $$\phi_i(\delta_i)\ge\frac{1-\delta_i/\lambda_i}{2\ln2}\ge\frac{\lambda_i-\delta_i}{2\theta\ln2}=-c(\delta_i-\lambda_i).$$ It holds at $\delta_i=0$ by the infinite-value convention. A zero eigenvalue has only $\delta_i=0$ and contributes zero. Thus for every feasible coordinate, $\phi_i(\delta_i)\ge\phi_i(\delta_i^*)-c(\delta_i-\delta_i^*)$, with $\delta_i^*=\min(\lambda_i,\theta)$.

Summing the supporting inequalities in step 2.1 and using $\sum_i\delta_i\le D=\sum_i\delta_i^*$ proves $\sum_i\phi_i(\delta_i)\ge\sum_i\phi_i(\delta_i^*)$. The latter sum is exactly $\frac12\sum_i\log_2^+(\lambda_i/\theta)$; the allocation is feasible, so it attains the minimum.

If $D=0$, nonnegativity forces every $\delta_i=0$, giving the two stated cases. If $D\ge\sum_i\lambda_i$, choose $\delta_i=\lambda_i$ for every i; all rates are zero, and no feasible objective can be negative. These cases complete the endpoint and degenerate branches.

Let $p_{XY}$ be a joint probability vector on finite alphabets $\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y$, with marginals $p_X(x):=\sum_y p_{XY}(x,y)$ and $p_Y(y):=\sum_xp_{XY}(x,y)$. The marginals are probability vectors by [[lem-it-finite-marginals-and-conditionals-are-pmfs]]. The joint vector is the outcome-weight function of the canonical finite probability space from [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]; its coordinate maps are finite random elements in the sense of [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]. Define mutual information in nats by

$$I(X;Y):=D(p_{XY}\|p_X\otimes p_Y)=\sum_{(x,y):p_{XY}(x,y)>0}p_{XY}(x,y)\ln\frac{p_{XY}(x,y)}{p_X(x)p_Y(y)},$$

where $D$ is the finite KL convention of [[def-qa-35-finite-probability-entropy-and-stochastic-matrices]] and $(p_X\otimes p_Y)(x,y):=p_X(x)p_Y(y)$. Every ratio in the displayed sum is positive and finite: if $p_{XY}(x,y)>0$, then each marginal sum is at least that positive entry. The sum is over finite support, so $I(X;Y)$ is finite. The base-$b$ version replaces $\ln$ by $\log_b$.

For any $b>1$, define each base-$b$ finite information quantity by replacing $\ln$ with $\log_b$ in its defining finite formula. Then

$$H_b(p)=\frac{H(p)}{\ln b},\qquad D_b(p\|q)=\frac{D(p\|q)}{\ln b},$$

where the second equality is in $[0,+\infty]$ and $+\infty/\ln b:=+\infty$. The same conversion holds for finite conditional entropy, mutual information, and conditional mutual information. In particular, values in bits equal nats divided by $\ln2$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

derivations.claim: For each $x$, choose a minimizing $\hat x_x$ from the nonempty finite set $\widehat{\mathcal X}$; finite choice is available by successive selection from finitely many nonempty sets. The deterministic channel $W(\hat x\mid x)=\mathbf1_{\{\hat x=\hat x_x\}}$ has expected distortion $D_{\min}$. Conversely, each channel row is a probability vector, so its conditional mean distortion is at least $\min_{\hat x}d(x,\hat x)$; averaging against $p$ shows every channel has distortion at least $D_{\min}$. Thus feasibility is equivalent to $D\ge D_{\min}$.

For a probability vector $q$, set $H(q)=-\sum_i q_i\ln q_i$, with $0\ln0:=0$. The scalar function $-t\ln t$ on $(0,1]$ extends continuously to zero because $\lim_{t\downarrow0}t\ln t=0$; hence entropy is continuous on every finite simplex. Expanding the finite KL sum in [F1] gives $I(X;\widehat X)=H(p)+H(q)-H(p_{X\widehat X})$, where $q(\hat x)=\sum_xp(x)W(\hat x\mid x)$; all terms are continuous functions of the channel coordinates.

Identify all channels with a point in $[0,1]^{|\mathcal X||\widehat{\mathcal X}|}$. The row-sum equalities, nonnegativity inequalities and expected-distortion inequality define a closed set; the cube makes it bounded. When feasible it is nonempty, so [F3] makes it compact.

By [F2], division by the positive constant $\ln2$ preserves continuity. Thus the bit mutual-information objective is continuous on the nonempty compact feasible set in step 2.1; [F4] gives a point where it attains its minimum. This proves attainment.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $X,Y$ be random elements with standard-Borel value spaces $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ and $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, and let $P_{XY}$, $P_X$, and $P_Y$ be their joint and marginal probability laws. The product law $P_X\otimes P_Y$ exists by [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]. Define the mutual information in nats by

$$I_{\mathrm{nat}}(X;Y):=D(P_{XY}\|P_X\otimes P_Y)\in[0,+\infty],$$

where $D$ is the directional Kullback–Leibler divergence of [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. This definition remains meaningful when one or both laws have no Lebesgue density and does not subtract differential entropies that may be infinite.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Let $E,F$ be standard-Borel spaces, let $\mu,
u$ be probability measures on E, and let $K,L:Eightsquigarrow F$ be probability kernels. Let $P=\mu\ltimes K$ and $Q=
u\ltimes L$ be the joint probability laws defined by
$$P(C)=\int_E K(x,C_x)\,\mu(dx),\qquad Q(C)=\int_E L(x,C_x)\,
u(dx)$$
for product-measurable $C\subseteq E	imes F$. Then
$$D(P\|Q)=D(\mu\|
u)+\int_E D(K(x,\cdot)\|L(x,\cdot))\,\mu(dx)=D(\mu\|
u)+D_\mu(K\|L),$$
as an equality in $[0,+\infty]$. In particular, when $\mu=
u$, the joint KL is the conditional KL from [[def-conditional-kl-for-probability-kernels]].

Assume AC and use the directional convention of
[[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. For probability measures $P,Q$ on one
measurable space, $D(P\|Q)\ge0$, and $D(P\|Q)=0$ if and only if $P=Q$.

There is also the following normalized-density identity. Let
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space: it is a set
with a sigma-algebra and measure ([[def-measure-space]]), and there is a
countable measurable cover by sets of finite $\mu$-measure
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]). Let
$\gamma:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable function with
$Z:=\int\gamma\,d\mu\in(0,\infty)$, and put $\pi=\gamma/Z$. Let
$q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable probability density,
so $\int q\,d\mu=1$, and suppose $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on
$\{\gamma=0\}$. Assume
$$\int q\bigl(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|\bigr)\,d\mu<\infty,$$
where each term with $q=0$ is defined to be zero. Then
$$\log Z =\int q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu +D(q\,\mu\|\pi\,\mu).$$
In particular, the first integral is at most $\log Z$. This identity concerns
normalized densities only; it does not assert posterior existence for an
unspecified statistical model.

derivations.claim: By [F2]–[F3], the laws $N(0,\sigma^2)$ and $N(y,D)$ have everywhere-positive Lebesgue densities $p_X(x)=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}$ and $q_y(x)=(2\pi D)^{-1/2}e^{-(x-y)^2/(2D)}$. Define $Q(dx,dy):=P_Y(dy)q_y(x)\,dx$; this is the joint law whose conditional law of $X$ given $Y=y$ is $N(y,D)$, with $Y$-marginal $P_Y$. Both $Q$ and $P_X\otimes P_Y$ are equivalent to $dx\,P_Y(dy)$, since their densities are strictly positive. If $P_{XY}\not\ll P_X\otimes P_Y$, [F1] and [F4] give $I_{\mathrm{nat}}(X;Y)=+\infty$, so the result holds. Otherwise equivalence gives $P_{XY}\ll Q$ as well.

On the remaining case, the logarithm of the reference-density ratio is $$\ln\frac{q_Y(X)}{p_X(X)}=\frac12\ln\frac{\sigma^2}{D}-\frac{(X-Y)^2}{2D}+\frac{X^2}{2\sigma^2}.$$ It is integrable because $\mathbb E(X-Y)^2=\delta<\infty$ and $\mathbb E X^2=\sigma^2$. The Radon–Nikodym chain identity $dP_{XY}/d(P_X\otimes P_Y)=(dP_{XY}/dQ)(dQ/d(P_X\otimes P_Y))$, integrated using [F4], therefore yields $$I_{\mathrm{nat}}(X;Y)=D(P_{XY}\|Q)+\frac12\ln\frac{\sigma^2}{D}+\frac12-\frac{\delta}{2D}.$$ The finite cross term prevents an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity if the first divergence is infinite.

Since $Q$ and $P_{XY}$ have the same $Y$-marginal, [F5] expresses $D(P_{XY}\|Q)$ as an integral of conditional KL divergences; [F6] makes it nonnegative, including the value $+\infty$. Also $\delta\le D$, so $1/2-\delta/(2D)\ge0$. The identity in step 2.1 gives the claimed lower bound.

Let $\mathcal X,\widehat{\mathcal X}$ be nonempty finite alphabets, let $p$ be a pmf on $\mathcal X$, and let $d:\mathcal X\times\widehat{\mathcal X}\to[0,\infty)$ be finite-valued. $$
R_{p,d}(D):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\min_{W:\,\mathbb E d(X,\hat X)\le D} I(X;\hat X),&D\ge D_{\min},\\[4pt]+\infty,&D<D_{\min}. \end{cases}
$$
The minimum exists by [[lem-it-finite-rate-distortion-minimum-attained]]. Values are not operational code rates; the finite memoryless coding theorem is a separate claim.

Let $\mathcal X,\widehat{\mathcal X}$ be nonempty finite sets, let $p$ be a probability mass function on $\mathcal X$, and let $d:\mathcal X\times\widehat{\mathcal X}\to[0,\infty)$ be finite-valued. Put
$$
D_{\min}:=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}p(x)\min_{\hat x\in\widehat{\mathcal X}}d(x,\hat x).
$$

$$\sum_{a_i>0}a_i\ln\frac{a_i}{b_i}\ge A\ln\frac AB.$$

When $A,B>0$, equality holds exactly when $a_i=(A/B)b_i$ for every $i$. If $A>0=B$, both sides are $+\infty$ and no finite equality characterization is asserted.

Let $\mathcal X,\widehat{\mathcal X}$ be nonempty finite alphabets, let $p$ be a pmf on $\mathcal X$, and let $d:\mathcal X\times\widehat{\mathcal X}\to[0,\infty)$ be finite-valued. A test channel is a stochastic matrix $W(\hat x\mid x)$, and its expected single-letter distortion is $\sum_{x,\hat x}p(x)W(\hat x\mid x)d(x,\hat x)$, with block distortion as in [[def-it-single-letter-distortion-and-block-distortion]]. Put $D_{\min}=\sum_xp(x)\min_{\hat x}d(x,\hat x)$. Define, in bits,
$$
R_{p,d}(D):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\min_{W:\,\mathbb E d(X,\hat X)\le D} I(X;\hat X),&D\ge D_{\min},\\[4pt]+\infty,&D<D_{\min}. \end{cases}
$$
The minimum exists by [[lem-it-finite-rate-distortion-minimum-attained]]. Values are not operational code rates; the finite memoryless coding theorem is a separate claim.

Let $p_{XY}$ be a joint probability vector on finite alphabets $\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y$, with marginals $p_X(x):=\sum_y p_{XY}(x,y)$ and $p_Y(y):=\sum_xp_{XY}(x,y)$. The marginals are probability vectors by [[lem-it-finite-marginals-and-conditionals-are-pmfs]]. The joint vector is the outcome-weight function of the canonical finite probability space from [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]; its coordinate maps are finite random elements in the sense of [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]. Define mutual information in nats by

$$I(X;Y):=D(p_{XY}\|p_X\otimes p_Y)=\sum_{(x,y):p_{XY}(x,y)>0}p_{XY}(x,y)\ln\frac{p_{XY}(x,y)}{p_X(x)p_Y(y)},$$

where $D$ is the finite KL convention of [[def-qa-35-finite-probability-entropy-and-stochastic-matrices]] and $(p_X\otimes p_Y)(x,y):=p_X(x)p_Y(y)$. Every ratio in the displayed sum is positive and finite: if $p_{XY}(x,y)>0$, then each marginal sum is at least that positive entry. The sum is over finite support, so $I(X;Y)$ is finite. The base-$b$ version replaces $\ln$ by $\log_b$.

For finite $X,Y,Z$,

$$I(X;Y|Z)=H(X|Z)+H(Y|Z)-H(X,Y|Z)\ge0.$$

Equality holds if and only if, for every $z$ with $p_Z(z)>0$, the conditional joint pmf factors as $p_{XY|z}=p_{X|z}p_{Y|z}$; this is conditional independence given $Z$.

For finite $X,Y,Z$ with a joint pmf,

$$H(X,Y|Z)=H(X|Z)+H(Y|X,Z),$$

and

$$I(X;Y,Z)=I(X;Z)+I(X;Y|Z).$$

In particular, $I(X;Y)=H(X)-H(X|Y)=H(Y)-H(Y|X)$. All terms are finite.
For finite probability vectors $p,q$ on the same alphabet, $D(p\|q)\ge0$, and $D(p\|q)=0$ if and only if $p=q$. If $p_i>0=q_i$ for some coordinate, then $D(p\|q)=+\infty$.

derivations.claim: Let $Y$ be any test-channel output and put $E=X\oplus Y$, where $\oplus$ is addition modulo two; write $e=\mathbb P(E=1)=\mathbb E d(X,Y)$. Since $X=Y\oplus E$, the map $(Y,E)\mapsto X$ is deterministic and bijective in E for each Y, so $H(X|Y)=H(E|Y)$. By [F4], $H(E)-H(E|Y)=I(E;Y)$, and this mutual information is nonnegative by [F3] and [F5]; hence $H(E|Y)\le H(E)=h_2(e)$. If $0\le D\le p_0\le1/2$ and $e\le D$, then $h_2(e)\le h_2(D)$: on $(0,1/2)$, $h_2'(u)=\log_2((1-u)/u)\ge0$, and continuity supplies the endpoints. The entropy identity in [F4] therefore gives $I(X;Y)\ge h_2(p)-h_2(D)$.

Suppose $0\le D\le p_0$ and $(p,D)\ne(1/2,1/2)$. Then $1-2D>0$ and $q:=(p-D)/(1-2D)\in[0,1]$: nonnegativity follows from $D\le p$ (since $D\le p_0$), while $q\le1$ is equivalent to $p+D\le1$, which follows from $D\le1-p$. Let $Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q)$, independently let $E\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(D)$, and set $X=Y\oplus E$. Then $\mathbb P(X=1)=q(1-D)+(1-q)D=D+q(1-2D)=p$, and the Hamming distortion is exactly $D$.

If $D\ge p_0$, reconstructing constantly by the more probable source symbol has expected Hamming distortion $p_0$ and zero mutual information; [F5] makes zero the minimum. This proves the formula on that branch, including deterministic sources.

Since E is independent of Y and determines X given Y, $H(X|Y)=H(E|Y)=H(E)=h_2(D)$. Thus $I(X;Y)=h_2(p)-h_2(D)$, attaining the converse in step 1.1. The excluded corner $p=1/2,D=1/2$ is covered by step 2.1. This proves the formula for all parameters.

Let $(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a stationary source on a finite nonempty alphabet $\mathcal X$, let $\widehat{\mathcal X}$ be finite nonempty, and let $d:\mathcal X\times\widehat{\mathcal X}\to[0,d_{\max}]$ be a bounded finite-valued distortion. For $n\ge1$ and $D\ge0$, define
$$
R_n(D):=\frac1n\min_{W_n:\,\mathbb E d_n(X_0^{n-1},\widehat X_0^{n-1})\le D} I(X_0^{n-1};\widehat X_0^{n-1})\quad\text{bits/symbol},
$$
with value $+\infty$ when the constraint is infeasible. The minimum is attained whenever feasible by [[lem-it-finite-rate-distortion-minimum-attained]] applied to the block alphabets. Put
$$
D_{\min}:=\mathbb E\min_{\hat x\in\widehat{\mathcal X}}d(X_0,\hat x),\qquad D_{\rm c}:=\min_{\hat x\in\widehat{\mathcal X}}\mathbb E d(X_0,\hat x),\qquad R_{\rm block}(D):=\inf_{n\ge1}R_n(D).
$$
The stationary-ergodic process information rate-distortion quantity is
$$
R_{\rm erg}(D):=\inf \limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n I(X_0^{n-1};\widehat X_0^{n-1}),
$$
where the infimum ranges over jointly stationary ergodic pairs of finite-alphabet processes with the given source marginal and $\mathbb E d(X_0,\widehat X_0)\le D$; an empty infimum is $+\infty$. The block-limit lemma proves $R_n(D)\to R_{\rm block}(D)$, convexity, and right continuity at $D_{\min}$.

$$I(X;Y):=D(p_{XY}\|p_X\otimes p_Y)=\sum_{(x,y):p_{XY}(x,y)>0}p_{XY}(x,y)\ln\frac{p_{XY}(x,y)}{p_X(x)p_Y(y)},$$

where $D$ is the finite KL convention of [[def-qa-35-finite-probability-entropy-and-stochastic-matrices]] and $(p_X\otimes p_Y)(x,y):=p_X(x)p_Y(y)$. Every ratio in the displayed sum is positive and finite: if $p_{XY}(x,y)>0$, then each marginal sum is at least that positive entry. The sum is over finite support, so $I(X;Y)$ is finite. The base-$b$ version replaces $\ln$ by $\log_b$.

For any $b>1$, define each base-$b$ finite information quantity by replacing $\ln$ with $\log_b$ in its defining finite formula. Then

$$H_b(p)=\frac{H(p)}{\ln b},\qquad D_b(p\|q)=\frac{D(p\|q)}{\ln b},$$

where the second equality is in $[0,+\infty]$ and $+\infty/\ln b:=+\infty$. The same conversion holds for finite conditional entropy, mutual information, and conditional mutual information. In particular, values in bits equal nats divided by $\ln2$.
Proves the finite-alphabet entropy chain rule and that conditioning on additional finite-valued variables cannot increase conditional entropy, in bits.

For finite $X,Y,Z$ with a joint pmf,

$$H(X,Y|Z)=H(X|Z)+H(Y|X,Z),$$

and

$$I(X;Y,Z)=I(X;Z)+I(X;Y|Z).$$

In particular, $I(X;Y)=H(X)-H(X|Y)=H(Y)-H(Y|X)$. All terms are finite.

Let $(a_i)_{i=1}^n,(b_i)_{i=1}^n$ be finite nonnegative real vectors, with $A=\sum_i a_i$ and $B=\sum_i b_i$. Interpret $\sum_{a_i>0}a_i\ln(a_i/b_i)$ as $+\infty$ if some $a_i>0=b_i$; otherwise zero coordinates contribute $0$. Interpret $A\ln(A/B)$ as $0$ if $A=0$ and as $+\infty$ if $A>0=B$. Then

$$\sum_{a_i>0}a_i\ln\frac{a_i}{b_i}\ge A\ln\frac AB.$$

When $A,B>0$, equality holds exactly when $a_i=(A/B)b_i$ for every $i$. If $A>0=B$, both sides are $+\infty$ and no finite equality characterization is asserted.

Let $\mathcal X,\widehat{\mathcal X}$ be nonempty finite sets, let $p$ be a probability mass function on $\mathcal X$, and let $d:\mathcal X\times\widehat{\mathcal X}\to[0,\infty)$ be finite-valued. Put
$$
D_{\min}:=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}p(x)\min_{\hat x\in\widehat{\mathcal X}}d(x,\hat x).
$$
For every $D\ge0$, the feasible stochastic channels $W(\hat x\mid x)$ satisfying $\sum_{x,\hat x}p(x)W(\hat x\mid x)d(x,\hat x)\le D$ form a nonempty set exactly when $D\ge D_{\min}$. Whenever nonempty, mutual information in bits attains its minimum over this set.

Let $X,Y,Z$ have a joint pmf on finite alphabets and suppose that, for every $y$ with $p_Y(y)>0$,

$$p_{XZ|y}(x,z)=p_{X|y}(x)p_{Z|y}(z).$$

This is the finite Markov condition $X\to Y\to Z$. Then

$$I(X;Z)\le I(X;Y),$$

with equality if and only if $I(X;Y|Z)=0$, equivalently $X$ and $Y$ are conditionally independent given every positive-mass value of $Z$.

derivations.claim: Write $a_n(D)=nR_n(D)$, and choose minimizing channels for blocks of lengths $m$ and $n$, available by [F5]. Use their conditional product as a channel on the concatenated block. Stationarity gives the same marginal laws for the second block as for a block of length $n$; each part has mean distortion at most $D$, so the concatenated normalized distortion is at most $D$.

A best constant reconstruction has normalized expected distortion $D_{\rm c}$ and zero mutual information for every block; nonnegativity of finite KL gives $R_n(D)=0$ for $D\ge D_{\rm c}$. If $D<D_{\min}$, every coordinate distortion is at least its pointwise minimum, so no block channel is feasible and each $R_n(D)=+\infty$.

Suppose $D_{\rm c}>D_{\min}$, and let $\gamma$ be the smallest positive value among the finite gaps $d(x,\hat x)-\min_zd(x,z)$; thus $\gamma>0$. Fix $0<\epsilon<\gamma/2$. Since $D_{\min}+\epsilon$ is feasible, [F5] supplies a minimizing length-$n$ channel at that distortion budget. Let $S_i=1$ when its chosen reproduction has positive gap from the pointwise minimum, and let $\alpha=n^{-1}\sum_i\mathbb P(S_i=1)$. The excess above the block minimum is at least $\gamma\sum_i S_i/n$, so $\alpha\le\epsilon/\gamma$.

Let $(X_1,Y_1)$ and $(X_2,Y_2)$ denote the two source/output block pairs under that channel. Conditional independence of the two channel outputs given the full source block gives $H(Y_1,Y_2\mid X_1,X_2)=H(Y_1\mid X_1)+H(Y_2\mid X_2)$. Entropy subadditivity gives $H(Y_1,Y_2)\le H(Y_1)+H(Y_2)$. Subtracting these finite quantities and using [F3] yields $I(X_1,X_2;Y_1,Y_2)\le I(X_1;Y_1)+I(X_2;Y_2)$, so $a_{m+n}(D)\le a_m(D)+a_n(D)$. The source blocks need not be independent.

Keep the selected channel's original reproduction at coordinates with $S_i=0$, and replace coordinates with $S_i=1$ by a pointwise minimizing symbol for the observed source letter; call the resulting reproduction $\widehat X'^n$. Its distortion is exactly $D_{\min}$ coordinatewise. The original output, flags, and correction symbols determine $\widehat X'^n$, so [F6] and the chain rule/entropy bounds give $$ I(X^n;\widehat X'^n)\le I(X^n;\widehat X^n)+H(S^n)+\sum_i\mathbb P(S_i=1)\log_2|\widehat{\mathcal X}|. $$ By entropy subadditivity and concavity of binary entropy, $H(S^n)\le n h_2(\alpha)$. Thus $R_n(D_{\min})\le R_n(D_{\min}+\epsilon)+h_2(\epsilon/\gamma)+(\epsilon/\gamma)\log_2|\widehat{\mathcal X}|$, since $h_2$ is increasing on $[0,1/2]$.

Fix $k\ge1$, write $n=qk+r$ with $0\le r<k$, and put $a_0=0$. Repeated subadditivity gives $a_n\le qa_k+a_r$. The finite set $\{a_r:0\le r<k\}$ is bounded, so $\limsup_n a_n/n\le a_k/k$. Taking the infimum over $k$, while $\inf_k a_k/k\le\liminf_n a_n/n$, proves $a_n/n\to\inf_k a_k/k$.

For each fixed $n$, the feasible block-channel sets are nested as $D$ increases, so $R_n(D)$ is nonincreasing. Mixing two block channels and applying [F4] shows $R_n$ is convex. Passing to the pointwise limit from step 3.1 preserves both monotonicity and the convexity inequality.

Taking infima over $n$ in step 2.2 gives the same inequality for $R_{\rm block}$. The two error terms tend to zero as $\epsilon\downarrow0$; monotonicity from step 4.1 gives the reverse bound $R_{\rm block}(D_{\min}+\epsilon)\le R_{\rm block}(D_{\min})$, proving right-continuity. If $D_{\rm c}=D_{\min}$, step 1.2 already gives zero on the entire feasible interval.

derivations.claim: Let a deterministic length-$n$ code have $M_n$ messages and reconstruction $\widehat X^n$. Data processing [F6] gives $I(X^n;\widehat X^n)\le H(f_n(X^n))\le\log_2M_n$. Put $D_n=\mathbb E d_n(X^n,\widehat X^n)$, and let $T$ be uniform on $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, independent of all variables; set $(X,Y)=(X_T,\widehat X_T)$. Since the source symbols are iid, $H(X^n)=\sum_iH(X_i)$. By [F5], the chain rule, and conditioning reducing entropy from [F7], $$ I(X^n;\widehat X^n)=\sum_i\bigl[H(X_i)-H(X_i\mid X^{i-1},\widehat X^n)\bigr]\ge\sum_i I(X_i;\widehat X_i). $$ Also $I(X;Y\mid T)=n^{-1}\sum_iI(X_i;\widehat X_i)$, while $I(X;T)=0$; the chain rule and nonnegative conditional information [F7] imply $I(X;Y)\le I(X;Y,T)=I(X;Y\mid T)$. Thus $R(D_n)\le I(X;Y)\le n^{-1}I(X^n;\widehat X^n)\le n^{-1}\log_2M_n$, since $\mathbb E d(X,Y)=D_n$.

Assume $D\ge D_{\min}$, and choose a minimizing test channel $W(\hat x|x)$ by [F3]. Let $Y$ have its induced output pmf, and let $(X_i,Y_i)$ be iid copies of the test-channel pair. Its information density $\imath(X;Y)=\log_2[W(Y|X)/P_Y(Y)]$, on positive joint support, is finite-valued because the alphabets are finite; it has mean $I:=R(D)$. The block distortion is bounded with mean at most $D$. The iid law of large numbers therefore gives, for every $\eta,\delta>0$, $$ \mathbb P\{d_n(X^n,Y^n)\le D+\eta,\ \sum_{i<n}\imath(X_i;Y_i)\le n(I+\delta)\}\longrightarrow1. $$ The distortion and information-density summands are bounded on finite alphabets, hence square-integrable; [F8] applied to each iid sequence proves both convergences in probability and the displayed joint event.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $\mathcal X,\widehat{\mathcal X}$ be standard-Borel spaces, let $P_X$ be a probability law on $\mathcal X$, and let $d:\mathcal X\times\widehat{\mathcal X}\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. A feasible joint law, or coupling, is a probability measure $\pi$ on $\mathcal X\times\widehat{\mathcal X}$ whose $\mathcal X$-marginal is $P_X$. Define

$$R_{\mathrm{std}}(D):=\inf_{\substack{\pi_{\mathcal X}=P_X\\ \int d\,d\pi\le D}}\frac{D(\pi\|P_X\otimes\pi_{\widehat{\mathcal X}})}{\ln2}=\inf_{\substack{\pi_{\mathcal X}=P_X\\ \int d\,d\pi\le D}}\frac{I_{\mathrm{nat}}(X;\widehat X)}{\ln2}.$$

No density for $Y$, conditional differential entropy, or subtraction of potentially infinite entropies is assumed.

$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,

$$I_{\rm nat}(X_i;Y^m\mid W_i)=I_{\rm nat}(X_i;Y_i\mid W_i)+I_{\rm nat}(X_i;Y_{[m]\setminus\{i\}}\mid W_i,Y_i)\ge I_{\rm nat}(X_i;Y_i\mid W_i),$$

If $D\ge\sum_i\lambda_i$, nonnegativity is the lower bound zero; the all-zero variance case has the same lower bound for every $D$.

For $\lambda_i>\theta$, put $a_i=\sqrt{\lambda_i-\theta}$, $b=\sqrt\theta$, and take independent standard normals $U_i,V_i$ using the finite product law in [F10]; set $Y_i=a_iU_i$, $X_i=a_iU_i+bV_i$. The orthogonal rotation with first row $(a_i,b)/\sqrt{\lambda_i}$ and [F9] gives the required $N(0,\lambda_i)$ source; the squared error has mean $b^2=\theta$. By [F6], [F7] and the product normal density, the joint density of $(X_i,Y_i)$ is $(2\pi a_ib)^{-1}\exp[-y_i^2/(2a_i^2)-(x_i-y_i)^2/(2b^2)]$; dividing by the product of the source and reconstruction densities gives expected log ratio $\frac12\ln(\lambda_i/\theta)$. Choose all coordinate pairs independently. Their joint and product-marginal laws factor, and the log density ratio is the sum of the coordinate log ratios, each integrable; [F1] therefore makes the vector mutual information the sum $\frac12\sum_i\ln^+(\lambda_i/\theta)$ nats. By [F1], the rate is this value divided by $\ln2$, so the construction attains the bit-valued lower bound.

If $D\ge\sum_i\lambda_i$, choose $Y=0$; the error is the total variance and mutual information is zero. If every $\lambda_i=0$, the same constant reconstruction has zero error and zero mutual information for all $D\ge0$. These constructions attain the remaining lower bounds and complete the proof.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Consider a finite nonempty alphabet $\mathcal A$, a probability measure $P$ on $\mathcal A^{\mathbb Z}$, and the left shift $T(x)_j=x_{j+1}$.

The shift is measurable on the product sigma-algebra. Call $P$ stationary when it is measure preserving under this shift, precisely the condition in [[def-measure-preserving-transformation-and-system]].

For a stationary $P$, call the source ergodic when each event $E$ satisfying $T^{-1}E=E$ has $P(E)\in\{0,1\}$; by [[def-ergodic-measure-preserving-system]] this is exactly ergodicity of the probability system.

Let $(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a stationary source on a finite nonempty alphabet $\mathcal X$, let $\widehat{\mathcal X}$ be finite nonempty, and let $d:\mathcal X\times\widehat{\mathcal X}\to[0,d_{\max}]$ be a bounded finite-valued distortion. For $n\ge1$ and $D\ge0$, define
$$
R_n(D):=\frac1n\min_{W_n:\,\mathbb E d_n(X_0^{n-1},\widehat X_0^{n-1})\le D} I(X_0^{n-1};\widehat X_0^{n-1})\quad\text{bits/symbol},
$$
with value $+\infty$ when the constraint is infeasible. The minimum is attained whenever feasible by [[lem-it-finite-rate-distortion-minimum-attained]] applied to the block alphabets. Put
$$
D_{\min}:=\mathbb E\min_{\hat x\in\widehat{\mathcal X}}d(X_0,\hat x),\qquad D_{\rm c}:=\min_{\hat x\in\widehat{\mathcal X}}\mathbb E d(X_0,\hat x),\qquad R_{\rm block}(D):=\inf_{n\ge1}R_n(D).
$$
The stationary-ergodic process information rate-distortion quantity is
$$
R_{\rm erg}(D):=\inf \limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n I(X_0^{n-1};\widehat X_0^{n-1}),
$$
where the infimum ranges over jointly stationary ergodic pairs of finite-alphabet processes with the given source marginal and $\mathbb E d(X_0,\widehat X_0)\le D$; an empty infimum is $+\infty$. The block-limit lemma proves $R_n(D)\to R_{\rm block}(D)$, convexity, and right continuity at $D_{\min}$.

For a stationary finite-alphabet source and bounded additive distortion as in [[def-it-stationary-finite-block-information-rdf]], the sequence $R_n(D)$ has a limit for every feasible $D$, and
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}R_n(D)=\inf_{n\ge1}R_n(D)=R_{\rm block}(D).
$$
The function $R_{\rm block}$ is nonincreasing and convex on $[D_{\min},\infty)$, is zero for $D\ge D_{\rm c}$, and is right-continuous at $D_{\min}$. It is infinite below $D_{\min}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For any set $I$, standard-Borel coordinate spaces $(E_i,\mathcal E_i)$, and consistent finite-dimensional laws $(\mu_F)_{F\Subset I}$, there is a unique probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal C_I$ whose $F$-coordinate marginal is $\mu_F$ for each finite $F$.

Let $(E,\mathcal E)$ and $(F,\mathcal F)$ be measurable spaces and let $P$ be a probability measure on $(E\times F,\mathcal E\otimes\mathcal F)$. Its marginals are $P_E(A)=P(A\times F)$ and $P_F(B)=P(E\times B)$. The product probability $P_E\otimes P_F$ exists by the finite product-measure theorem. Define the **measure-theoretic mutual information** of the joint law $P$ by
$$I(P):=D(P\|P_E\otimes P_F)\in[0,+\infty].$$
For random elements $X,Y$ with joint law $P_{XY}$, write $I(X;Y):=I(P_{XY})$. The logarithm convention is the natural logarithm, so finite values are in nats as fixed by [[def-it-information-units-and-logarithm-base]]. The divergence is directional in its two law arguments and is $+\infty$ when $P_{XY}\not\ll P_X\otimes P_Y$.

This definition uses only the joint law, not a choice of density or a difference of entropy quantities.

For standard-Borel random elements X,Y,Z,
$$I((Z,X);Y)=I(Z;Y)+I(X;Y\mid Z).$$
The right side is a sum in $[0,+\infty]$. This chain rule is asserted as an equality of extended nonnegative quantities; no difference of possibly infinite entropies or divergences occurs.

Let X,Y,Z be random elements with standard-Borel value spaces and joint law $P_{XYZ}$. Let $K(z,\cdot)$ and $L(z,\cdot)$ be regular conditional laws of X and Y given Z=z. Let R be the probability law on the product space whose rectangle values are
$$R(C\times A\times B)=\int_C K(z,A)L(z,B)\,P_Z(dz).$$
Its existence, uniqueness, and independence of the versions K,L are established in [[lem-same-marginal-conditional-product-law-well-defined]]. Define the **conditional mutual information** by
$$I(X;Y\mid Z):=D(P_{XYZ}\|R)\in[0,+\infty].$$
The reference R has the same Z marginal as the joint law and makes X,Y independent conditionally on Z. The logarithm is natural, so finite values are measured in nats under [[def-it-information-units-and-logarithm-base]]. The definition is a divergence between full probability laws; it does not subtract two possibly infinite entropies.

Let $\phi:(E,\mathcal E)\to(F,\mathcal F)$ be a measurable bijection with measurable inverse. For probability measures P,Q on E, let $\phi_\#P,\phi_\#Q$ be their push-forwards. Then
$$D(\phi_\#P\|\phi_\#Q)=D(P\|Q).$$

Let $X,Y,Z$ have a joint pmf on finite alphabets and suppose that, for every $y$ with $p_Y(y)>0$,

$$p_{XZ|y}(x,z)=p_{X|y}(x)p_{Z|y}(z).$$

This is the finite Markov condition $X\to Y\to Z$. Then

$$I(X;Z)\le I(X;Y),$$

with equality if and only if $I(X;Y|Z)=0$, equivalently $X$ and $Y$ are conditionally independent given every positive-mass value of $Z$.

Let $\mu$ be sigma-finite, let $T$ preserve $\mu$, and let $f$ be a
finite-valued real- or complex-valued measurable representative in
$\mathcal L^1(\mu)$.  Then $A_nf$ converges $\mu$-almost everywhere to a
finite-valued integrable function $f^*$ satisfying

$$f^*\circ T=f^*\quad\mu\text{-almost everywhere},\qquad \lVert f^*\rVert_1\leq\lVert f\rVert_1.$$

The a.e. class of $f^*$ depends only on the a.e. class of $f$.  No ergodicity,
finite total measure, completeness, or invertibility is assumed.

derivations.claim: By [F2]–[F3], choose $k\ge1$ and a length-$k$ test channel $W_k$ whose expected normalized distortion is at most $D$. Write $I_k:=I_2(X_0^{k-1};\widehat X_0^{k-1})$ bits for this channel and $r_k:=I_k/k$. The choice can be made with $r_k<r$ because $R_{\rm block}(D)=\inf_kR_k(D)<r$ and the finite-block minimum is attained.

Fix $p\in(0,1)$. By [F4], the consistent finite-dimensional product laws of a mutually independent family $(B_t,U_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$, with each $B_t\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ and each $U_t$ uniform on $[0,1]$, extend to a probability law $P_M$ on their two-sided sequence space. In particular the marker and seed processes are independent. Let $(\Omega_X,P_X,T)$ be the source shift system and form the independent product extension $(\Omega_X\times\Omega_M, P_X\otimes P_M,T\times S)$, where $S$ is the marker-seed shift. The product measure exists by the probability product-measure theorem in the dependency closure of [F5], and its rectangle formula makes the source independent of both marker and seed processes. Almost surely there are marker times $B_t=1$ arbitrarily far in both directions: for each fixed starting index, the probability of no marker in the next $N$ sites is $(1-p)^N\to0$, and a countable union handles all starting indices. Thus the marker set partitions $\mathbb Z$ into finite segments between consecutive markers.

The product of the source system and the iid marker-seed shift is ergodic. To verify this, take two bounded real-valued rectangle cylinder functions $f_1(X)g_1(B,U)$ and $f_2(X)g_2(B,U)$. For all sufficiently large shifts $n$, the iid-coordinate windows of $g_1$ and $g_2\circ S^n$ are disjoint, so their expectation factors as $\mathbb E g_1\,\mathbb E g_2$. For the source factor, [F7] gives almost-sure convergence of $N^{-1}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}f_2(T^nX)$ to a finite invariant function $f_2^*$. Ergodicity makes $f_2^*$ constant almost surely: for each rational $a$, the limsup orbit set $\limsup_{n\to\infty}T^{-n}\{f_2^*>a\}$ is strictly invariant and differs from $\{f_2^*>a\}$ by a null set, so it has probability zero or one; the rational level sets then force a constant value. Since $f_2$ is bounded, dominated convergence and preservation of the source law show this constant is $\mathbb E f_2$. Thus the time averages of $f_2$ converge almost surely to $\mathbb E f_2$, and bounded convergence gives $$ \frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\mathbb E[f_1(X)f_2(T^nX)]\longrightarrow\mathbb E f_1\,\mathbb E f_2. $$ The Cesàro correlations of the rectangle functions therefore converge to the product of their means. Their finite linear combinations are dense in real product $L^2$: indicators of measurable rectangles form a generating $\pi$-system, and the class of sets whose indicators lie in the $L^2$-closure of their span is a Dynkin class, since increasing unions converge in $L^2$ on a probability space. The $\pi$-$\lambda$ theorem and density of simple functions give the claim. Cauchy–Schwarz and shift invariance extend the correlation limit to every real $L^2$ function. If $A$ is invariant, its indicator has correlation $\mathbb P(A)$ at every shift, while the limit is $\mathbb P(A)^2$; hence $\mathbb P(A)\in\{0,1\}$.

For a segment beginning at a marker $s$ and ending just before the next marker $s+L$, divide its first $k\lfloor L/k\rfloor$ sites into consecutive length-$k$ blocks. At each such block start use its seed $U_t$ and the finite inverse-cumulative rule to sample an output block from $W_k(\cdot\mid X_t^{t+k-1})$. On the remaining $L\bmod k<k$ sites, output a fixed pointwise minimizing reproduction $\hat x_*(X_t)$. This defines $\widehat X$ measurably and commutes with shifts because the same marker, block, seed, and tie-breaking rules are used at every translated location.

The pair $(X,\widehat X)$ is a shift-commuting factor of the ergodic product system from step 1.3, so it is stationary and ergodic: the preimage of a shift-invariant event in the factor is shift-invariant in the product and therefore has probability zero or one. Its source marginal is unchanged because the construction leaves X fixed.

Let $\alpha$ be the probability that coordinate zero lies in a leftover suffix. A segment of length $\ell$ has $\ell\bmod k$ leftover sites. Summing over its possible start and length gives $$ \alpha=p^2\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}(\ell\bmod k)(1-p)^{\ell-1}\le(k-1)p^2\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}(1-p)^{\ell-1}=(k-1)p. $$ Marker events in this sum specify a cut at the segment start, no intervening marker, and a cut at the end; the leftover site is one of the final $\ell\bmod k$ positions.

The marker process is independent of X. For any length-$n$ window, condition on the markers and sum distortion over all test-channel blocks fully contained in the window; each such block has the stationary length-$k$ source law, so its expected total distortion is at most $kD$. At most two blocks intersect the window without being contained, and their total distortion is bounded by $2k d_{\max}$. Leftover sites have expected distortion $D_{\min}$ each. Divide by $n$, take expectations, and let $n\to\infty$; the boundary contribution vanishes, while stationarity makes the expected mean distortion equal to $\mathbb E d(X_0,\widehat X_0)$ for every n. Since the expected leftover fraction is $\alpha$, this yields $\mathbb E d(X_0,\widehat X_0)\le(1-\alpha)D+\alpha D_{\min}\le D$.

Let E be the independent marker process B, leaving the independent uniform seeds unconditioned. Its value space $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb Z}$ is standard Borel. Put $U=X_0^{n-1}$ and $V=\widehat X_0^{n-1}$. Independence in step 1.2 gives $P_{UE}=P_U\otimes P_E$, so $I_2(U;E)=D(P_U\otimes P_E\|P_U\otimes P_E)/\ln2=0$. Coordinate-swap invariance and the first-argument chain rule in [F5] now give
$$I_2(U;(V,E))=I_2((E,V);U)=I_2(E;U)+I_2(V;U\mid E)=0+I_2(U;V\mid E).$$
Expanding instead in the order $(V,E)$ gives $I_2(U;(V,E))=I_2(U;V)+I_2(U;E\mid V)\ge I_2(U;V)$. Thus $I_2(X_0^{n-1};\widehat X_0^{n-1})\le I_2(X_0^{n-1};\widehat X_0^{n-1}\mid E)$, using only nonnegative extended sums and the explicitly zero independent term. Conditional on E, outputs from distinct test-channel blocks are sampled independently according to $W_k$, and leftover outputs are deterministic. Enlarge the source window to include every source coordinate in a full length-$k$ block intersecting $[0,n-1]$, and enlarge the output to include each such full test-channel block output plus the leftover reconstructions inside the window. The original source and output windows are coordinate projections of these enlarged finite vectors, so [F6], applied conditionally on each marker realization, bounds the original information by the enlarged information. Conditional output entropy is subadditive across block outputs and leftover symbols. Given the enlarged source and E, the block outputs are independent and the leftover symbols are deterministic, so conditional output entropy is the sum of the block conditional entropies. Each length-$k$ block has the stationary source law followed by $W_k$, and hence contributes $I_k$ bits; each leftover symbol contributes at most $\log_2|\widehat{\mathcal X}|$ bits. There are at most $n/k+2$ intersecting channel blocks, and stationarity makes the expected number of leftover sites in the window $n\alpha$. Therefore $$ \frac1n I_2(X_0^{n-1};\widehat X_0^{n-1})\le\left(\frac1k+\frac2n\right)I_k+\alpha\log_2|\widehat{\mathcal X}|. $$

Since $r_k<r$, choose $p>0$ small enough that $(k-1)p\log_2|\widehat{\mathcal X}|<r-r_k$ (if the logarithm is zero, any $p\in(0,1)$ works). Taking $n\to\infty$ in step 4.2 and using step 3.2 yields a limiting upper information rate at most $r_k+(k-1)p\log_2|\widehat{\mathcal X}|<r$. Steps 3.1 and 4.1 give the required stationary ergodic pair and distortion bound.

For the exact-real recurrence, let $p_1,\ldots,p_m>0$ be source probabilities summing to one, let $d_{ij}\ge0$ be finite distortions on a nonempty finite reproduction alphabet $[n]$, let $\beta\ge0$ be finite, and let $q_0$ be any full-support reproduction pmf. For $t=0,1,\ldots$ set
$$
Z_i(q_t)=\sum_{j=1}^n q_t(j)e^{-\beta d_{ij}},\qquad W_t(j\mid i)=\frac{q_t(j)e^{-\beta d_{ij}}}{Z_i(q_t)},\qquad q_{t+1}(j)=\sum_{i=1}^m p_iW_t(j\mid i).
$$
All denominators are positive, every row of $W_t$ sums to one, and $q_{t+1}$ has full support. Define the nats objective $L_\beta(W)=I_{\rm nat}(X;\widehat X)+\beta\mathbb E d(X,\widehat X)$, the current channel value $L_t=L_\beta(W_t)$, and the a-posteriori factor
$$
\gamma_t:=\max_{1\le j\le n}\sum_{i=1}^m p_i\frac{e^{-\beta d_{ij}}}{Z_i(q_t)}\ge1.
$$

For tolerance $\tau>0$, the output is the first processed iteration index $t$ for which the interval procedure below certifies an upper bound $u_t\ge\ln\gamma_t$ with $u_t\le\tau$, together with the current channel $W_t$, its output law $q_{t+1}$, its objective value $L_t$, and interval enclosures of these values and of $\ln\gamma_t$. The exact-real recurrence defines the values being enclosed; the returned intervals are required to contain them.

The certified interval procedure has the following representability conditions: every $p_i$, $d_{ij}$, $\beta$, every coordinate of $q_0$, and $\tau$ is a rational input, with the positivity, normalization, and finiteness conditions above and $\tau>0$. At iteration $t$, evaluate the finite recurrence and objective with outward-rounded intervals, refining precision until the enclosures of all output values and $\ln\gamma_t$ have width less than $1/(t+1)$. If the resulting rational upper endpoint $u_t$ for $\ln\gamma_t$ is at most $\tau$, return the stated output; otherwise proceed to iteration $t+1$. Positive denominators and finite distortions make each finite calculation well-defined. For arbitrary exact-real inputs the recurrence remains mathematically defined, but this interval implementation is specified only under the rational representability conditions. No bit-complexity bound is asserted.

Let $p_{XY}$ be a joint probability vector on finite alphabets $\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y$, with marginals $p_X(x):=\sum_y p_{XY}(x,y)$ and $p_Y(y):=\sum_xp_{XY}(x,y)$. The marginals are probability vectors by [[lem-it-finite-marginals-and-conditionals-are-pmfs]]. The joint vector is the outcome-weight function of the canonical finite probability space from [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]; its coordinate maps are finite random elements in the sense of [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]. Define mutual information in nats by

$$I(X;Y):=D(p_{XY}\|p_X\otimes p_Y)=\sum_{(x,y):p_{XY}(x,y)>0}p_{XY}(x,y)\ln\frac{p_{XY}(x,y)}{p_X(x)p_Y(y)},$$

where $D$ is the finite KL convention of [[def-qa-35-finite-probability-entropy-and-stochastic-matrices]] and $(p_X\otimes p_Y)(x,y):=p_X(x)p_Y(y)$. Every ratio in the displayed sum is positive and finite: if $p_{XY}(x,y)>0$, then each marginal sum is at least that positive entry. The sum is over finite support, so $I(X;Y)$ is finite. The base-$b$ version replaces $\ln$ by $\log_b$.
For finite probability vectors $p,q$ on the same alphabet, $D(p\|q)\ge0$, and $D(p\|q)=0$ if and only if $p=q$. If $p_i>0=q_i$ for some coordinate, then $D(p\|q)=+\infty$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

derivations.claim: For every reproduction pmf $q$, including boundary points of the simplex, define $G(W,q):=\sum_i p_iD(W(\cdot|i)\|q)+\beta\mathbb E d$, where a row divergence is $+\infty$ if that row puts positive mass outside the support of $q$. Since each $p_i>0$, $G(W,q)$ is finite only when every row is supported on $\{j:q(j)>0\}$. Also $Z_i(q)>0$ for every pmf $q$, because $e^{-\beta d_{ij}}>0$ and $q$ has total mass one. Define $W_q(j|i)=q(j)e^{-\beta d_{ij}}/Z_i(q)$, which is zero off that support. For every supported row, expansion of finite KL sums gives $$D(W(\cdot|i)\|q)+\beta\sum_jW(j|i)d_{ij}=D(W(\cdot|i)\|W_q(\cdot|i))-\ln Z_i(q).$$ Nonnegativity [F3] shows that $W_q$ minimizes each row; unsupported rows have infinite objective and cannot improve it. Therefore $F(q):=\min_WG(W,q)=-\sum_i p_i\ln Z_i(q)$ on the closed simplex. If $q_W$ is the output law of $W$, expansion on the common support gives $G(W,q)=L_\beta(W)+D(q_W\|q)$ when $q_W$ is supported on $q$; otherwise both sides are $+\infty$.

The channel simplex is closed and bounded in finite-dimensional Euclidean space, hence compact by [F4]. The finite mutual-information objective is continuous by its entropy expression and continuity of $-u\ln u$ at zero; distortion is linear. Thus [F5] gives a minimizer $W^*$. Put $q^*=q_{W^*}$, $P^*(i,j)=p_iW^*(j|i)$. Step 1.1 gives $G(W,q)\ge L_\beta(W)\ge L_\beta^*$ for every $W,q$, while $G(W^*,q^*)=L_\beta^*$ because $q^*$ is the output marginal of $W^*$. Therefore $F(q^*)=L_\beta^*$ and $q^*$ minimizes the boundary-extended $F$.

For each iterate set $P_t(i,j)=p_iW_t(j|i)$. The identities in step 1.1 give $$ F(q_t)=L_t+D(q_{t+1}\|q_t),\qquad F(q_{t+1})\le G(W_t,q_{t+1})=L_t. $$ Consequently $L_{t+1}\le F(q_{t+1})\le L_t$: the objective sequence is nonincreasing.

Expand the finite joint divergence using the update formula for $W_t$: $$ D(P^*\|P_t)=L_\beta^*+D(q^*\|q_t)-F(q_t). $$ Indeed $\ln W_t(j|i)=\ln q_t(j)-\beta d_{ij}-\ln Z_i(q_t)$; multiplying $\ln(W^*/W_t)$ by $p_iW^*_{ij}$ and summing gives the displayed identity. Marginalizing the joint laws over the reproduction coordinate and expanding the finite conditional sums gives $$ D(P^*\|P_t)=D(q^*\|q_{t+1})+\sum_{j:q^*_j>0}q^*_jD(P^*(X\in\cdot\mid j)\|P_t(X\in\cdot\mid j))\ge D(q^*\|q_{t+1}), $$ where [F3] supplies nonnegativity. Thus $F(q_t)-L_\beta^*\le D(q^*\|q_t)-D(q^*\|q_{t+1})$. Since $L_t\le F(q_t)$, the same upper bound holds for $L_t-L_\beta^*$.

Define $s_j(q_t)=\sum_i p_i e^{-\beta d_{ij}}/Z_i(q_t)=q_{t+1,j}/q_{t,j}$. For $a_{ij}=e^{-\beta d_{ij}}/Z_i(q_t)$, concavity of $\ln$ and $F(q^*)=L_\beta^*$ give $$ F(q_t)-L_\beta^*=\sum_i p_i\ln\left(\sum_jq_j^*a_{ij}\right) \le\ln\left(\sum_jq_j^*s_j(q_t)\right)\le\ln\max_js_j(q_t)=\ln\gamma_t. $$ Since $L_t\le F(q_t)$, this proves the stated a-posteriori certificate. Step 4.1 gives $L_t\to L_\beta^*$; the first identity in step 2.2 then gives $F(q_t)\to L_\beta^*$. The simplex is compact, and $F$, each $s_j$, and $\gamma$ are continuous there because every $Z_i(q)\ge\min_j e^{-\beta d_{ij}}>0$. Every cluster point of $q_t$ is therefore a minimizer of $F$.

At any minimizer $q$ of differentiable $F(q)=-\sum_i p_i\ln Z_i(q)$, the coordinate derivative is $-s_j(q)$. Moving mass between a positive coordinate and any other coordinate shows $s_j(q)=1$ on the support and $s_j(q)\le1$ off the support; the active value equals one because $\sum_jq_js_j(q)=1$. Hence $\gamma(q)=1$ at every minimizer. Compactness and continuity from step 5.1 imply $\gamma_t\to1$: otherwise a subsequence bounded away from one would have a cluster point with the same property. Thus $\ln\gamma_t\to0$, and every positive tolerance is eventually met. The argument permits zero coordinates in $q^*$, so boundary minimizers are included.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X_0,X_1,\ldots$ be a source over a finite alphabet $\mathcal X$, let $\widehat{\mathcal X}$ be finite, and let $d$ be finite-valued. An $n$-block fixed-length code with $M_n$ messages is a deterministic encoder $f_n:\mathcal X^n\to[M_n]$ and decoder $g_n:[M_n]\to\widehat{\mathcal X}^{\,n}$; its reconstruction is $\widehat X^n=g_n(f_n(X^n))$, its block distortion is [[def-it-single-letter-distortion-and-block-distortion]], and its rate is $n^{-1}\log_2M_n$ bits per source symbol.

Define the expected-distortion operational rate $R_{\mathrm{op}}^{\mathrm{avg}}(D)$ as the infimum of $\limsup_n n^{-1}\log_2M_n$ over code sequences satisfying $\limsup_n\mathbb E d_n(X^n,\widehat X^n)\le D$. Define the positive-slack excess-distortion operational rate $R_{\mathrm{op}}^{\mathrm{slack}}(D)$ by the same rate infimum over code sequences satisfying

$$\text{for every }\varepsilon>0,\qquad \mathbb P\!\left(d_n(X^n,\widehat X^n)>D+\varepsilon\right)\longrightarrow0.$$

The expected and positive-slack excess criteria are separate definitions. An exact-threshold condition $\mathbb P(d_n>D)\to0$ is not part of either definition.

Let $(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a stationary source on a finite nonempty alphabet $\mathcal X$, let $\widehat{\mathcal X}$ be finite nonempty, and let $d:\mathcal X\times\widehat{\mathcal X}\to[0,d_{\max}]$ be a bounded finite-valued distortion. For $n\ge1$ and $D\ge0$, define
$$
R_n(D):=\frac1n\min_{W_n:\,\mathbb E d_n(X_0^{n-1},\widehat X_0^{n-1})\le D} I(X_0^{n-1};\widehat X_0^{n-1})\quad\text{bits/symbol},
$$
with value $+\infty$ when the constraint is infeasible. The minimum is attained whenever feasible by [[lem-it-finite-rate-distortion-minimum-attained]] applied to the block alphabets. Put
$$
D_{\min}:=\mathbb E\min_{\hat x\in\widehat{\mathcal X}}d(X_0,\hat x),\qquad D_{\rm c}:=\min_{\hat x\in\widehat{\mathcal X}}\mathbb E d(X_0,\hat x),\qquad R_{\rm block}(D):=\inf_{n\ge1}R_n(D).
$$
The stationary-ergodic process information rate-distortion quantity is
$$
R_{\rm erg}(D):=\inf \limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n I(X_0^{n-1};\widehat X_0^{n-1}),
$$
where the infimum ranges over jointly stationary ergodic pairs of finite-alphabet processes with the given source marginal and $\mathbb E d(X_0,\widehat X_0)\le D$; an empty infimum is $+\infty$. The block-limit lemma proves $R_n(D)\to R_{\rm block}(D)$, convexity, and right continuity at $D_{\min}$.

For a stationary finite-alphabet source and bounded additive distortion as in [[def-it-stationary-finite-block-information-rdf]], the sequence $R_n(D)$ has a limit for every feasible $D$, and
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}R_n(D)=\inf_{n\ge1}R_n(D)=R_{\rm block}(D).
$$
The function $R_{\rm block}$ is nonincreasing and convex on $[D_{\min},\infty)$, is zero for $D\ge D_{\rm c}$, and is right-continuous at $D_{\min}$. It is infinite below $D_{\min}$.

Assume AC. Let $(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a stationary ergodic source on a finite alphabet $\mathcal X$, let $\widehat{\mathcal X}$ be finite nonempty, and let $d:\mathcal X\times\widehat{\mathcal X}\to[0,d_{\max}]$ be bounded. For any feasible $D\ge D_{\min}$ and any $r>R_{\rm block}(D)$, there is a jointly stationary ergodic pair $(X_t,\widehat X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ with the given source marginal, $\mathbb E d(X_0,\widehat X_0)\le D$, and
$$
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n I_2(X_0^{n-1};\widehat X_0^{n-1})<r\quad\text{bits per symbol},
$$
where $I_2:=I_{\rm nat}/\ln2$ for the measure-theoretic mutual information of [[def-measure-theoretic-mutual-information]].
For a stationary ergodic finite-alphabet source, the componentwise information-rate limit is the constant entropy rate.

Let $\mu$ be sigma-finite, let $T$ preserve $\mu$, and let $f$ be a
finite-valued real- or complex-valued measurable representative in
$\mathcal L^1(\mu)$.  Then $A_nf$ converges $\mu$-almost everywhere to a
finite-valued integrable function $f^*$ satisfying

$$f^*\circ T=f^*\quad\mu\text{-almost everywhere},\qquad \lVert f^*\rVert_1\leq\lVert f\rVert_1.$$

The a.e. class of $f^*$ depends only on the a.e. class of $f$.  No ergodicity,
finite total measure, completeness, or invertibility is assumed.

Let $X,Y,Z$ have a joint pmf on finite alphabets and suppose that, for every $y$ with $p_Y(y)>0$,

$$p_{XZ|y}(x,z)=p_{X|y}(x)p_{Z|y}(z).$$

This is the finite Markov condition $X\to Y\to Z$. Then

$$I(X;Z)\le I(X;Y),$$

with equality if and only if $I(X;Y|Z)=0$, equivalently $X$ and $Y$ are conditionally independent given every positive-mass value of $Z$.

For finite $X,Y,Z$ with a joint pmf,

$$H(X,Y|Z)=H(X|Z)+H(Y|X,Z),$$

and

$$I(X;Y,Z)=I(X;Z)+I(X;Y|Z).$$

In particular, $I(X;Y)=H(X)-H(X|Y)=H(Y)-H(Y|X)$. All terms are finite.
Proves that n^{-1}H(X_0,...,X_{n-1}) converges under stationarity and equals the limit of the finite-past conditional entropies.

Let $p_{XY}$ be a joint probability vector on finite alphabets $\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y$, with marginals $p_X(x):=\sum_y p_{XY}(x,y)$ and $p_Y(y):=\sum_xp_{XY}(x,y)$. The marginals are probability vectors by [[lem-it-finite-marginals-and-conditionals-are-pmfs]]. The joint vector is the outcome-weight function of the canonical finite probability space from [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]; its coordinate maps are finite random elements in the sense of [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]. Define mutual information in nats by

$$I(X;Y):=D(p_{XY}\|p_X\otimes p_Y)=\sum_{(x,y):p_{XY}(x,y)>0}p_{XY}(x,y)\ln\frac{p_{XY}(x,y)}{p_X(x)p_Y(y)},$$

where $D$ is the finite KL convention of [[def-qa-35-finite-probability-entropy-and-stochastic-matrices]] and $(p_X\otimes p_Y)(x,y):=p_X(x)p_Y(y)$. Every ratio in the displayed sum is positive and finite: if $p_{XY}(x,y)>0$, then each marginal sum is at least that positive entry. The sum is over finite support, so $I(X;Y)$ is finite. The base-$b$ version replaces $\ln$ by $\log_b$.

For finite $X,Y,Z$ with a joint pmf,

$$H(X,Y|Z)=H(X|Z)+H(Y|X,Z),$$

and

$$I(X;Y,Z)=I(X;Z)+I(X;Y|Z).$$

In particular, $I(X;Y)=H(X)-H(X|Y)=H(Y)-H(Y|X)$. All terms are finite.

derivations.claim: For any source word $x_0^{n-1}$, every reconstruction word satisfies $$ d_n(x_0^{n-1},\hat x_0^{n-1})\ge\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\min_{\hat x}d(x_i,\hat x). $$ The right side has expectation $D_{\min}$ by stationarity, so every code has expected distortion at least $D_{\min}$. If $D<D_{\min}$, choose $\epsilon>0$ with $D+\epsilon<D_{\min}$ and put $g(X)=\min_{\hat x}d(X,\hat x)$. Birkhoff [F6] gives almost-sure convergence of the averages of this bounded function to a finite invariant function $g^*$. For every rational $a$, the limsup orbit set $\limsup_{n\to\infty}T^{-n}\{g^*>a\}$ is strictly invariant and differs from $\{g^*>a\}$ by a null set. Ergodicity makes each such level set have probability zero or one, so $g^*$ is constant almost surely. Dominated convergence and stationarity identify the constant as $\mathbb E g=D_{\min}$. Hence the pointwise-minimum block average converges almost surely to $D_{\min}$, and the probability that any code's distortion exceeds $D+\epsilon$ tends to one. Both operational criteria are therefore infeasible below $D_{\min}$. By [F2], no stationary coupling with mean distortion below $D_{\min}$ exists either, so $R_{\rm erg}(D)=+\infty$; [F3] gives $R_{\rm block}(D)=+\infty$.

Let a deterministic length-$n$ code have $M_n$ messages and reconstruction $\widehat X^n$. Since $X^n\to f_n(X^n)\to\widehat X^n$ is a Markov chain, [F7] gives $I(X^n;\widehat X^n)\le H(f_n(X^n))\le\log_2M_n$. Its induced joint law is feasible in the definition of $R_n(D_n)$, where $D_n=\mathbb E d_n(X^n,\widehat X^n)$, so $R_n(D_n)\le n^{-1}\log_2M_n$.

For every jointly stationary ergodic pair feasible at $D$, the finite-block law is feasible in $R_n(D)$, so $R_n(D)\le n^{-1}I_2(X_0^{n-1};\widehat X_0^{n-1})$. Taking limits and then the infimum over such pairs gives $R_{\rm block}(D)\le R_{\rm erg}(D)$.

For expected-distortion codes with $\limsup D_n\le D$, eventually $D_n\le D+\epsilon$, giving $R_n(D+\epsilon)\le n^{-1}\log_2M_n$. For a positive-slack excess code, boundedness gives $D_n\le D+\epsilon+d_{\max}\mathbb P(d_n>D+\epsilon)$, so eventually $D_n\le D+2\epsilon$; then $R_n(D+2\epsilon)\le n^{-1}\log_2M_n$. Taking limits and using [F3], followed by right-continuity as $\epsilon\downarrow0$, proves $R_{\rm block}(D)\le R_{\rm op}^{\rm avg}(D)$ and $R_{\rm block}(D)\le R_{\rm op}^{\rm slack}(D)$.

Conversely, for any bit rate $r>R_{\rm block}(D)$, [F4] supplies a jointly stationary ergodic pair with mean distortion at most $D$ and limsup bit mutual-information rate less than $r$. Thus $R_{\rm erg}(D)\le r$; letting $r\downarrow R_{\rm block}(D)$ proves $R_{\rm erg}(D)=R_{\rm block}(D)$.

Fix a jointly stationary ergodic pair $(X,\widehat X)$ supplied by step 2.2. By [F8], each of the source, reproduction, and joint-pair normalized block entropies has a limit; [F9] therefore gives convergence of $n^{-1}I_2(X_0^{n-1};\widehat X_0^{n-1})$ to a finite bit rate $\bar I\le\limsup n^{-1}I_2(X_0^{n-1};\widehat X_0^{n-1})<r$. By [F5] applied to those three stationary ergodic processes, their normalized negative log probabilities in bits converge almost surely to their entropy rates. Subtracting the three limits shows that the information density $$ i_n(x^n;\hat x^n):=\log_2\frac{P_{\widehat X^n|X^n}(\hat x^n|x^n)}{P_{\widehat X^n}(\hat x^n)} $$ divided by $n$ converges almost surely to $h(X)+h(\widehat X)-h(X,\widehat X)=\bar I$, with each entropy rate in bits.

On the ergodic pair shift let $g=d(X_0,\widehat X_0)$. By [F6], its time averages converge almost surely to a finite invariant function $g^*$. Apply the rational-level-set argument from step 1.1 to this bounded function on the ergodic pair system; its limit is constant, and dominated convergence with stationarity identifies that constant as $\bar d:=\mathbb E d(X_0,\widehat X_0)\le D$. Thus $d_n(X^n,\widehat X^n)\to\bar d$ almost surely. Fix $\eta>0$ and $\delta>0$. The event $$ G_n:=\{d_n(X^n,\widehat X^n)\le D+\eta,\ i_n(X^n;\widehat X^n)\le n(\bar I+\delta)\} $$ has probability tending to one by step 3.1 and this distortion convergence. Hence the set of source words whose conditional probability of this event is at least $1/2$ has source probability tending to one: its complement probability is at most twice $\mathbb P(G_n^c)$.

For any such source word $x^n$, on its good reproduction set the likelihood ratio $P_{\widehat X^n|x^n}/P_{\widehat X^n}$ is at most $2^{n(\bar I+\delta)}$. Therefore an independent reproduction word sampled from $P_{\widehat X^n}$ lands in that set with probability at least $\frac12 2^{-n(\bar I+\delta)}$. Draw $M_n=\lceil2^{n(\bar I+2\delta)}\rceil$ independent reproduction words. The probability that none works for this source word is at most $(1-q)^{M_n}\le e^{-M_nq}\le e^{-2^{n\delta}/2}$. Averaging over source words shows the expected failure probability of the random codebook tends to zero.

Some deterministic realization of each random codebook has failure probability at most twice its ensemble mean (if the mean is zero, choose a realization with zero failure). Encode a source word by the first codeword satisfying the good conditions, and use a fixed default reproduction if none does. The decoder outputs the selected codeword, so the code is deterministic and has $M_n$ messages. On success its distortion is at most $D+\eta$; on failure it is at most $d_{\max}$.

To obtain expected distortion at most $D$ in the limit and positive-slack excess distortion, choose a decreasing sequence $\eta_j\downarrow0$. For each $j$, the failure probability in step 6.1 is at most $1/j$ for all sufficiently large $n$; choose increasing thresholds and at each length use the largest such $j=j(n)$ available. Then $j(n)\to\infty$, expected distortion is at most $D+\eta_{j(n)}+d_{\max}/j(n)$, and for every fixed slack $\epsilon>0$, eventually $\eta_{j(n)}<\epsilon$, so $\mathbb P(d_n>D+\epsilon)\le1/j(n)\to0$. The code rate has limsup at most $\bar I+2\delta$.

Given any target rate $R_{\rm block}(D)+\epsilon$, choose $r=R_{\rm block}(D)+\epsilon/3$. Step 2.2 gives $\bar I<r$, so choose $\delta>0$ with $\bar I+2\delta<R_{\rm block}(D)+\epsilon$. Steps 5.1, 6.1 and 7.1 give both operational criteria at rate below the target. Thus $R_{\rm op}^{\rm avg}(D)\le R_{\rm block}(D)$ and $R_{\rm op}^{\rm slack}(D)\le R_{\rm block}(D)$. Together with steps 2.1 and 2.2 this proves all equalities. The excess criterion used positive slack throughout; it does not imply the unclaimed exact-threshold assertion at $D_{\min}$.

Assume AC. Let $\mathcal X,\widehat{\mathcal X}$ be standard-Borel spaces, let $P_X$ be a probability law on $\mathcal X$, and let $d:\mathcal X\times\widehat{\mathcal X}\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. A feasible joint law, or coupling, is a probability measure $\pi$ on $\mathcal X\times\widehat{\mathcal X}$ whose $\mathcal X$-marginal is $P_X$. Define

$$R_{\mathrm{std}}(D):=\inf_{\substack{\pi_{\mathcal X}=P_X\\ \int d\,d\pi\le D}}\frac{D(\pi\|P_X\otimes\pi_{\widehat{\mathcal X}})}{\ln2}=\inf_{\substack{\pi_{\mathcal X}=P_X\\ \int d\,d\pi\le D}}\frac{I_{\mathrm{nat}}(X;\widehat X)}{\ln2}.$$

The infimum of an empty feasible set is $+\infty$. Values are in bits. This definition makes no general existence or attainment claim and supplies no operational coding theorem for arbitrary standard-Borel alphabets.

Assume AC. Let $X,Y$ be random elements with standard-Borel value spaces $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ and $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, and let $P_{XY}$, $P_X$, and $P_Y$ be their joint and marginal probability laws. The product law $P_X\otimes P_Y$ exists by [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]. Define the mutual information in nats by

$$I_{\mathrm{nat}}(X;Y):=D(P_{XY}\|P_X\otimes P_Y)\in[0,+\infty],$$

where $D$ is the directional Kullback–Leibler divergence of [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. This definition remains meaningful when one or both laws have no Lebesgue density and does not subtract differential entropies that may be infinite.

$$
R(D)=\begin{cases}+\infty,&D=0,\\[2pt]\frac12\log_2^+(\sigma^2/D),&D>0,\end{cases}
$$
where $\log_2^+(u)=\max(0,\log_2u)$. If $\sigma^2=0$, then $R(D)=0$ for every $D\ge0$.

to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

Let $m\ge1$, let $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m\ge0$, and for $0\le\delta_i\le\lambda_i$ put

$$\phi_i(\delta_i):=\begin{cases}\frac12\log_2(\lambda_i/\delta_i),&\lambda_i>0,\ 0<\delta_i\le\lambda_i,\\+\infty,&\lambda_i>0,\ \delta_i=0,\\0,&\lambda_i=0,\ \delta_i=0.\end{cases}$$

For a total distortion budget $D\ge0$, minimize $\sum_i\phi_i(\delta_i)$ subject to $\sum_i\delta_i\le D$ and $0\le\delta_i\le\lambda_i$. If $0<D<\sum_i\lambda_i$, there is a unique $\theta\in(0,\max_i\lambda_i)$ satisfying

$$\sum_i\min(\lambda_i,\theta)=D,$$

and the minimum is
